children: By Ryan Felton
Early one morning on a recent weekday, Amber Nguyen was driving her 2025 Lexus SUV on a highway to a work meeting when she heard a loud bang.
"I'm not even joking, it sounded like a gunshot," said Nguyen, 26, who lives in Louisiana. "The sound is totally different than if a rock just hits your car."
The next thing she heard was a wind noise coming from above. The sunroof in Nguyen's Lexus shattered. Had the sunshade not been closed, she might have been covered in glass.

The experience is far from limited to her particular vehicle. Thousands of drivers have filed complaints with U.S. auto-safety regulators describing jarring incidents in which their sunroof unexpectedly exploded or shattered, often while they were driving. The number of complaints has soared recently and is set to hit a record in 2026, with nearly 500 reported so far this year.

The descriptions of those incidents listed in a federal database are harrowing: A Kia minivan's sunroof spontaneously exploded on a Wisconsin highway. A GMC sport-utility vehicle's moonroof fell onto seats where children ride. A Mercedes-Benz owner heard a "gunshot" sound like Nguyen-a frequent descriptor of these events, according to federal reports-before their car's glass ruptured.

The causes of these failures are similarly widespread. Road debris that drivers don't notice is one culprit, car designers and testers say. Hot temperatures and rapid temperature shifts can cause rapid expansions of the glass. Sometimes, design and manufacturing defects are to blame.

The sunroof failure reports target all major automakers, including 17 different manufacturers and more than 200 models over the past three years, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis. Roughly one-in-five complaints lodged in that time involved 2025 or 2026 model year vehicles, the analysis showed. Such failures happen roughly once a day.
Even so, the issues have rarely resulted in recall campaigns. Regulators say factors other than safety defects, such as road debris, are typically responsible for these events.
A spokesperson for the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said that it hasn't identified any verified crashes or serious injuries caused by breaking sunroofs.
"A breaking sunroof can be startling and costly, and NHTSA has investigated and is monitoring this issue," the spokesperson said.

It is enough to put drivers like Nguyen off owning a car with the feature. "If there was an option to get my car without a sunroof, I would've done it," she said. "I do love my car overall, everything about it, besides that."

Modern, motor-driven sunroofs rose in popularity in the 1980s. Initially a feature relegated to the luxury market, sunroofs are now equipped on more than 50% of vehicles produced for the U.S. market, up from 35% a decade prior, according to data from industry-research firm Omdia.
Some have fixed coverings that retract; others, often called "moonroofs," are single pieces of glass. (The two terms are often used interchangeably; reports about shattering include both.)

David Smith, a former design manager at General Motors, said sunroofs present an engineering challenge: cutting a hole out of a car's roof while maintaining the vehicle's stability and integrity. The feature has become more widespread as automakers eliminated common early issues, like leaking water and wind noise.
"They know how to build them pretty good now," Smith, a professor at the College for Creative Studies transportation design program, said of carmakers today.

David Bennett, automotive director for roadside assistance organization AAA, said the pieces of glass have grown larger in recent years, making them more vulnerable to road debris damage. Additional stress on the glass can result from vehicles operating on uneven roads or being exposed to the elements for extended periods, he said.

NHTSA has investigated these issues before. In 2013, the agency opened a probe into Kia Sorento SUVs in response to numerous reports from drivers of unexpected sunroof breakage. That investigation spanned seven years and roped in more than a dozen other automakers, identifying over 4,000 reports of sunroof fractures.

NHTSA ultimately said, in 2021, that it didn't find sufficient evidence of a safety-related defect, pointing instead to potential factors such as small rocks kicked up by other vehicles causing "imperceptible" damage that can eventually result in breakage.

The agency said federal regulations allow sunroofs to be made with tempered glass, which must break into gravel-like pieces, or laminated glass, where pieces stay stuck to a plastic interlayer instead of scattering. Manufacturers generally choose tempered glass, a spokesman said.
NHTSA also said major suppliers appeared to be moving toward using laminated glass and other improved materials. Those changes should reduce the incidents of glass breakage in the future.
Since 2021, NHTSA has received nearly 2,800 complaints of sunroofs unexpectedly exploding, of which more than 500 involve newer vehicles, according to the Journal's analysis.
Among the vehicles most commonly cited in recent years include Toyota's RAV4, the Hyundai Palisade SUV, the Kia Telluride SUV, and the Honda CR-V.

Hyundai said it continues to monitor the issue and will take action if a product defect is identified. The automaker has commissioned multiple studies to analyze sunroof breakage, it said, but hasn't found an inherent defect as a cause, only issues related to foreign objects impacting the glass.

Honda said it takes all consumer complaints seriously, but contends it hasn't seen a significant trend in complaints about the CR-V glass damage attributable to safety defects. A large number of CR-Vs sold have been equipped with a moonroof, including 95% this year as standard equipment, so comparing raw complaint numbers may fail to reflect actual occurrence rates of breakage, the company said.
Kia and Toyota declined to comment.

Jake Fisher, senior director at Consumer Reports' automotive test center, said carmakers can be doing more to prevent sunroofs from abruptly shattering. Laminated glass prevents windshields from breaking spontaneously, he said, and sunroofs should be able to withstand similar pressure.
"Ultimately there should be a more robust solution for it," he said.
